teaser: In 1865, Parisians came to laugh at her. She is still staring them down.

lesson.text: They laughed. They pointed with umbrellas and walking sticks. Some shouted. When Olympia went on show at the Paris Salon of 1865, the crowd in front of it was so thick and so hostile that the organizers worried for the canvas itself.

The newspapers joined in. One critic called her “a sort of female gorilla”. Others wrote that her skin was dirty, her body a corpse, the whole thing a bad joke. Manet, 33, wrote to his friend the poet Baudelaire: “Insults rain down on me like hail.”
Partway through the exhibition, the painting was moved to the last room and hung high above a doorway, where it was hard to see and harder to reach.

The strange part: the Salon was full of naked women that year, as every year. Nobody minded them. They were called Venus or nymph, they floated in clouds or woods, and they looked dreamily away. So what exactly did Manet do differently? The answers are small, and they are all on her body.

lesson.title: Four reasons for a scandal
lesson.text: Start with her face and work down.

spots.title: The look
spots.text: Level, cool, a little bored. She is not surprised to be seen. She is checking who just walked in, and that visitor is you.

spots.title: The ribbon
spots.text: A thin black ribbon tied in a bow, with a pearl. A goddess wears nothing at all. A ribbon makes her a modern woman who has undressed.

spots.title: The hand
spots.text: Spread flat and firm on her thigh. In older nudes this hand rests softly. Here it says: not unless I decide. Critics hated this hand more than anything.

spots.title: The slipper
spots.text: A satin house slipper, half off the foot. Like the gold bracelet and the earrings, it places her in a Paris bedroom, not on Mount Olympus.

lesson.text: Add those up and every visitor in 1865 understood. This was a courtesan, a woman paid by wealthy men, receiving a client. Even the name fit: “Olympia” was a nickname such women often used. Paris had thousands of them. Painting one life size, without excuse, was the offense.

Manet was not making it up as he went. He was quoting a famous Renaissance picture, Titian's Venus of Urbino, which he had copied in Florence as a young man. Same pose, same bed, same servant in the background. At the feet of Titian's Venus sleeps a little dog, an old symbol of faithfulness.
Manet swapped the faithful dog for another animal. It is hard to see. Where is it?

spots.title: The black cat
spots.text: Back arched, tail straight up, yellow eyes fixed on you. Black on a dark ground, it nearly vanishes. Cartoonists of 1865 adored it, and it became the emblem of the scandal.

lesson.text: The cat is startled, as if someone has just come in. The same arrival explains the bouquet. A maid is bringing flowers, still in their paper, presumably sent by an admirer. Olympia does not even glance at them.
The model was Victorine Meurent, then about 19, who posed for many of Manet's key pictures of the 1860s. She became a painter herself and had her own work accepted at the Salon.

Subject was only half the problem. The other half was paint. Academic nudes were shaded with endless soft transitions so the flesh looked like polished marble. Manet lit his model from the front, hard, and wiped out the half-tones, the in-between greys that make a form look round.
See how bluntly the picture is put together.

lines.label: The edge
lines.text: The gold border of the screen drops straight down the canvas and stops just above her hand. The room's architecture points at the very spot people complained about.

lines.label: The pale shape
lines.text: Her body reads as one pale shape with a dark contour, laid on the picture almost like a paper cutout. Viewers trained on soft shading found it flat and unfinished.

lines.label: Light below, dark above
lines.text: Roughly, the canvas splits in two: creamy whites below, near-black above. Very little sits in between.

lesson.text: Olympia shocked twice: by showing a real woman of 1863 instead of a goddess, and by painting her in flat, frank patches of light and dark. Many later painters took that double honesty as a starting point.

There is a second woman here, and for a long time few people wrote about her. Manet's notebook records her only by a first name, Laure, and an address in Paris. Slavery had been abolished in the French colonies just fifteen years earlier. Today historians study her as closely as Olympia.

spots.title: Laure
spots.text: Her face is turned toward her mistress, waiting for an answer that does not come. Her dark skin against the dark wall is painted with real care for its tones.

spots.title: The bouquet
spots.text: Quick dabs of white, blue and red inside a cone of paper. Up close it is nearly abstract. Step back and it becomes flowers.

spots.title: Flower in her hair
spots.text: A large pink bloom pinned behind her ear, another touch of finery for someone who is otherwise wearing a ribbon and a bracelet.

spots.title: The bracelet
spots.text: A heavy gold band with a dark pendant hanging from it. One of the few warm, solid objects against all that white linen.

spots.title: The shawl
spots.text: An embroidered silk shawl with flowers and a fringe, spread under her like a luxury wrapper. Its cream color is barely distinct from her skin.

spots.title: The pillows
spots.text: Whites painted with greys and blues, in broad, visible strokes. Manet loved the challenge of white on white.

lesson.text: Nobody bought the painting. It stayed in Manet's studio until his death in 1883, and then with his widow. When word spread in 1889 that an American collector might take it abroad, Claude Monet decided that France was not going to lose it.

Monet spent months writing to artists, writers and collectors, and raised nearly 20,000 francs by public subscription. In 1890 the group bought Olympia from Madame Manet and offered it to the French state, which hesitated before accepting.

The state sent her to the museum for living artists, not the Louvre. She only reached the Louvre in 1907, where she was hung beside the great nudes she had once been accused of insulting. The crowd that came this time was quiet.

quiz.question: How did the public react to Olympia at the Salon of 1865?
quiz.explanation: Visitors jeered, and the painting was moved high above a doorway.

quiz.question: Which older painting was Manet quoting?
quiz.explanation: He borrowed the pose, bed and servant from Titian's Venus, which he had copied in Florence.

quiz.question: What replaced the sleeping dog of the older picture?
quiz.explanation: The arched black cat at the foot of the bed became the emblem of the scandal.

quiz.question: What are “half-tones”, which Manet largely removed?
options: The in-between greys that make a form look round
Sketch lines left under the paint
quiz.explanation: By lighting the model from the front and dropping the soft transitions, he made the body look flat.

quiz.question: Who organized the purchase of Olympia for France in 1890?
quiz.explanation: Monet raised nearly 20,000 francs by public subscription.

quiz.question: What does the maid bring into the room?
quiz.explanation: The flowers, still wrapped, suggest an admirer has just sent them.

facts.text: Olympia sold quickly to a collector after the Salon of 1865.
facts.explanation: Nobody bought it; it stayed with Manet and then his widow until 1890.

facts.text: The model for Olympia, Victorine Meurent, later became a painter herself.
facts.explanation: She had her own work accepted at the Salon.

facts.text: Olympia entered the Louvre the same year the state accepted it.
facts.explanation: It went first to the museum for living artists and reached the Louvre only in 1907.
